profile.lead: I turn messy company knowledge into AI tools that people use every day.
profile.text: I spent four years at the LEGO Group, where I built MIND, an AI assistant used by 331 engineers to search their technical documentation. Now I build AI tools for teaching and research at Aarhus University, and I am looking for my next role in software, AI or digitalization.

docs.x: Philip Lau is currently Research Assistant, Aarhus University. Open to roles in software, AI and digitalization.

I joined the LEGO Group as an intern in 2022. Then I stayed three more years as a student worker in Mould Engineering. I built apps and automated workflows on the Power Platform and set up how they were tested and released. I also took MIND, an AI search assistant, from prototype towards a product. Since January 2026 I have been a Research Assistant at Aarhus University. I build AI tools, including one with the company EIVA. I also supervise three MSc projects and teach master's students to build AI business cases. My degrees are in business development. So I start with the problem and what it costs the business, and then I build the solution myself.

I work where technology meets the business. I start with the problem and what it costs, build the smallest thing that solves it, and stay until people use it. Most of my work deals with knowledge that is hard to find, such as manuals, standards, course material and research papers. I turn it into tools that answer questions and show where each answer comes from.
Next, I want to build AI and software full time, and over the years grow into shaping technology strategy.
Open to roles in Software engineering, AI and LLM development, Digitalization engineering, Forward deployed engineering and Technical project management.
Speaks Danish and English. Interests: Technology, Computer games, Marvel, LEGO and Olympic weightlifting. Based in Herning, Denmark.

docs.x: MIND is used by 331 engineers at the LEGO Group to search their technical documentation. It covers core documentation for element, mould development and mould construction. The proof of concept was estimated to save 240 hours.
docs.s: MIND: AI Search Assistant for LEGO Engineers

docs.x: Retrieval is hybrid. BM25 keyword search finds exact technical terms, and dense vector search finds passages with the same meaning in different words. The results are merged, and a cross-encoder reranker orders them. A query-rewriting step improves the search query. The language model answers only from the top passages and adds inline references, so each answer links back to its source passage. The measured results, the code and the evaluations are covered by a non-disclosure agreement with the LEGO Group, so I cannot share them here. I am happy to explain the design and the evaluation method in an interview. Technologies: RAG, Hybrid retrieval, BM25, Vector search, Reranking, Query rewriting.
docs.s: MIND: AI Search Assistant for LEGO Engineers

docs.t: TraceableAI: Literature Reviews With Checked Citations
docs.x: TraceableAI: Literature Reviews With Checked Citations. Literature reviews written by AI, where every citation can be checked. For each cited sentence, it shows the passage in the paper that supports it, or says plainly that it found none. (ongoing project, Aarhus University)
docs.s: TraceableAI: Literature Reviews With Checked Citations

docs.s: TraceableAI: Literature Reviews With Checked Citations

docs.t: TraceableAI: Literature Reviews With Checked Citations
docs.x: A literature review reads the published research on a question and sums up what it says, citing each paper it relies on. Ask a language model to review the literature, and you get fluent text with citations that are often wrong, mismatched or invented. Researchers cannot trust a review they cannot check.
docs.s: TraceableAI: Literature Reviews With Checked Citations

docs.t: TraceableAI: Literature Reviews With Checked Citations
docs.x: A web app that runs a full PRISMA 2020 systematic review. You type a research question and your criteria. It writes the review protocol before it searches, searches open scholarly databases, screens every record twice, reads the open-access full texts and groups the findings into themes. Then it writes the report and checks every citation against the paper it cites.
docs.s: TraceableAI: Literature Reviews With Checked Citations

docs.t: TraceableAI: Literature Reviews With Checked Citations
docs.x: The paper is accepted at OSSYM 2026, the 8th International Open Search Symposium at CODE University in Berlin. The tool is open source under Apache 2.0, live on its own website, and each release is archived with a DOI on Zenodo.
docs.s: TraceableAI: Literature Reviews With Checked Citations

docs.x: ASP.NET Core and Blazor on .NET 10, in C#. The model is Mistral through its API, or a local model through Ollama. The code is grouped by review stage: Sources (arXiv, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Crossref, and Scopus and IEEE Xplore with a key), Search, Screening, Evidence, Synthesis, Verification and Report. Every model answer is JSON that is validated in code. A citation verdict counts only when its supporting quote is found word for word in the paper. A sentence that claims more than its source is rewritten and checked again, and an unsupported citation is removed. Counts, the methods section and the PRISMA flow diagram are written by code from what the run did, never by the model. Screening runs twice with independent prompts, and agreement is reported as Cohen's kappa. Each run keeps its protocol, raw database responses, every decision and every model call on file, fingerprinted with SHA-256 and downloadable as one archive with a LaTeX manuscript and BibTeX and RIS files. Text from papers is treated as data: hidden text is stripped and phrases that try to steer the model are flagged. Other tools can start a review through a REST API or an MCP server. The xUnit tests run offline against a scripted fake model. Technologies: C#, .NET 10, Blazor, Mistral, PRISMA 2020, Citation checking, Open source.
docs.s: TraceableAI: Literature Reviews With Checked Citations

docs.t: Open Door: A Classroom Game for Threat Modelling
docs.x: A team game for one class of 45 or 90 minutes. Teams walk around Nordknit, a made-up Danish clothing business, talk to staff, look closer at things like the Wi-Fi router, and stick notes where they see a risk. Then an incident plays out, such as a fake e-mail that changes the bank details, and each team votes on what the CEO should do. Students join with a code on the projector, with no accounts. The teacher runs the class from one page, can send hints, and ends the session, which deletes everything.
docs.s: Open Door: A Classroom Game for Threat Modelling

docs.x: TypeScript in three workspaces: a Svelte 5 app built with Vite, a Cloudflare Worker that hosts live sessions, and shared game rules and messages. Each session is a Durable Object that holds the game state and applies the rules; browsers connect to it over a WebSocket, and the projector page watches the same room without changing it. The office map is drawn in SVG inside Svelte. Scenarios are plain YAML files checked against a JSON schema, so teachers can write new ones without coding, and printable paper kits are built from the same files. Security follows the game's own method: rate limits on session creation and lookups, a per-connection message limit, origin checks, a random teacher key kept in the URL fragment, a content security policy, and deletion of all data when the session ends or after six hours. Tested with Vitest and Playwright, including accessibility checks with axe. Code under MIT, content under CC BY-SA 4.0, building on the CyPro method from Aarhus University. Technologies: TypeScript, Svelte, Cloudflare Workers, WebSockets, Threat modelling, Game-based learning, Open source.

docs.x: Philip's role on LUMA: Personal project, sole developer.
I wanted one assistant for chat, news, music and commands that runs on my own computer instead of in the cloud.
LUMA has five tools on a bar at the bottom of the screen: a live news and markets feed, a chat window for voice or text, a camera view, a command terminal and a music player connected to Spotify.
A working desktop app that answers with a local model today. Version 1 is public on GitHub. The current version is private.

The frontend is a PyQt6 desktop app built around a central animated core and five modules on a bottom dock. World Feed shows a live TV stream, a market ticker and chart, a top story and headlines. Chat takes voice or text and uses draggable glass-style panels. Optic shows the live camera. Terminal runs Luma's own commands and skills. Music shows what is playing on Spotify and controls playback. Replies come from a local model through Ollama today. Later, I plan to swap in LUMA Brain, the small language model I am building from scratch. The source code is private. Technologies: Python, PyQt6, Ollama, Voice and wake word, Local AI, Spotify, Desktop UI.
